newsitem.title: INDIA: India's RBI seen revamping bank credit delivery.
newsitem.headline: India's RBI seen revamping bank credit delivery.

text.p: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) is expected to announce steps to improve credit delivery in its forthcoming credit policy but the existing system may not be replaced at one stroke, bankers and analysts said.
The RBI releases its credit and monetary policy for the first half of 1997/98 (April-March) on April 15.
"We expect some modification in the existing system of calculating maximum permissible bank finance," said P.H Ravikumar, senior vice-president at ICICI Banking Corporation.
Maximum permissible bank finance (MPBF) is a means of determining the maximum working capital limits a borrower can avail from banks.

Under the existing dispensation, the RBI sets individual and industry-wise inventory and receivables norms which banks have to adhere to while calculating the working capital loan limits for borrowers.
Introduced as a means of assessing loan limits uniformly and in a prudent manner, the system may have outgrown its usefulness to banks and borrowers alike, analysts said.
"The concept is not wrong," said Sanjay Dalal, general manager (finance) at textiles firm Arvind Mills Ltd.
"It means assessment of bank finance for working capital requirements in a prudent manner," he said.
Dalal said the system should be flexible and not reduced to straitjacket formulas.
"Over a period of time, it has however been reduced to a standard formula which does not take cognisance of the nature of business and business cycles," Dalal said.

In a meeting with RBI governor Chakravarty Rangarajan on Tuesday to discuss issues relating to the monetary policy, a team of economists said the efficiency of the financial sector also played a role in determining interest rates.

"It is necessary to address issues relating to credit delivery system such as the concept of maximum permissible bank finance and consortium lending in order to accelerate the flow of credit," a statement issued after the meeting said.
"Banks need to be given greater freedom to determine limits for their borrowers," said a senior banker at a state-run bank who declined to be identified.
"But I don't think it is going to be removed at one go," Ravikumar said.
"I think what will happen is that banks will be allowed to do away with the MPBF norms for big borrowers," he said.
"The criteria for determining big borrowers could be either size of assets, business turnover or exisitng limits," he added.
Banking analyst Amit Rajpal of Prime Broking agreed saying that removal of the existing system could result in chaos in the banking industry.
"All of a sudden you cannot ask people (bankers) who are used to determining limits according to a certain formula to change overnight," Rajpal said.
"The phase-out will have to be in stages."
